```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Conventional regression analysis assumes that a single set of relationships
between an outcome and its predictors applies uniformly across all
observations. Mixture regression models relax this assumption by allowing the
population to consist of a finite number of unobserved subgroups (latent
classes), each characterized by its own regression function. Rather than
estimating a single regression equation for the entire sample, the model
simultaneously estimates class-specific regression coefficients, the relative
size of each class, and the posterior probability of class membership for
each observation. This allows for the identification of unobserved
heterogeneity in the relationships between predictors and outcomes. Mixture
regression is also referred to as clusterwise regression, latent class
regression, or regression mixture modelling (DeSarbo & Cron, 1988; Wedel &
DeSarbo, 1995).

Conceptually, mixture regression extends the person-centred perspective of
latent profile analysis from identifying subgroups based on patterns of
indicator values to identifying subgroups based on patterns of relationships
among variables. Whereas latent profile analysis distinguishes individuals
according to their response patterns or indicator means, mixture regression
distinguishes them according to how the outcome relates to its predictors.
Thus, individuals belonging to different latent classes may exhibit different
regression coefficients, indicating that the same predictor can have
different associations with the outcome across subgroups (Scrucca et al.,
2024; Saqr et al., 2024).

`mixture_regression()` fits it for continuous (`"gaussian"`), binary or binomial
(`"binomial"`), count (`"poisson"`, and `"negative_binomial"` for overdispersed
counts) and ordered (`"ordinal"`, cumulative logit) outcomes, at one level or
two:

| Question | Call |
|---|---|
| Do observations follow different regressions? | `mixture_regression(y ~ x, data, n_classes)` |
| Do *groups* (persons, schools) follow different regressions? | `mixture_regression(..., id = "person", class_level = "group")` |
| Do groups differ in how often their observations follow each regression? | `mixture_regression(..., id = "person", n_group_classes = 2)` |
| What predicts which class an observation (or group) is in? | `membership = ~ z`, `group_membership = ~ v` |
| Is some effect the same in every class? | `common = ~ x2` |
| How many classes? | `enumerate_regressions(..., n_classes = 1:4)` |

## The data

`study_hours` is simulated so that the truth is known. 150 students report
six weeks each. In each week a student studies with a *deep* or a *surface*
strategy, and the strategy determines how hours translate into a quiz score: deep
weeks gain about 4.5 points per hour from a base of 35, and surface weeks
less than one point per hour from a base of 55. Steady students study deeply in most weeks,
erratic students in few. The generating strategy and student type are kept in
the data so recovery can be checked; the models never see them.

```{r data}
library(latents)
head(study_hours)
```

## One class per observation

```{r single}
fit <- mixture_regression(score ~ hours, data = study_hours, n_classes = 2,
                          n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
fit
```

The two classes correspond to the two strategies. Class 1, 56.4% of the
weeks, has a steep regression from a low base (4.57 points per hour from
34.36), and class 2, 43.6%, a flat regression from a high base (0.81 points
per hour from 54.90). Relative entropy is only 0.443: at few hours of study
the two regressions predict similar scores, so many weeks cannot be assigned
with confidence. Every table comes from `get_results()`; the
class table gives each class's share, its residual standard deviation and how
certainly its members are assigned.

```{r classes}
get_results(fit, "classes")
```

`get_results(fit, "assignments")` gives one row per observation. Because
these data carry the generating strategy, the recovery table cross-tabulates
the assigned classes against it:

```{r recovery}
get_results(fit, "recovery", data = study_hours, truth = "strategy")
```

Class 1 contains 78.2% deep weeks and class 2 85.0% surface weeks, so both
regressions are recovered, with the misclassification that the low entropy
implies.

```{r plot-fitted}
plot(fit)
```

## The number of classes

`enumerate_regressions()` fits a range of class counts and returns their fit
statistics in one table, marking the minimum-BIC model.

```{r enumerate}
classes <- enumerate_regressions(score ~ hours, data = study_hours,
                                 n_classes = 1:4, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
classes
```

The BIC is lowest for two classes (6,336, against 6,510 for one, 6,341 for
three and 6,354 for four), and the three-class model adds a class of only
7.5% of the weeks.

With `bootstrap = B`, each row also gets a parametric bootstrap
likelihood-ratio test of one class fewer (McLachlan 1987): outcomes are
simulated from the smaller model, both models are refitted, and the p-value
is `(b + 1) / (B + 1)`, where `b` is the number of simulated statistics at
least as large as the observed one.
It is slow, requiring `2 B` refits per row, and is therefore not run here.

## Predictors of class membership

`membership` adds a multinomial logit for class membership. Here sleep before
the quiz makes a deep week more likely, so it should lower the odds of the
surface class:

```{r membership}
with_sleep <- mixture_regression(score ~ hours, data = study_hours, n_classes = 2,
                                 membership = ~ sleep, n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(with_sleep, "membership")
```

Each additional hour of sleep multiplies the odds of a surface week by 0.77
(95% interval of the log odds -0.45 to -0.07). The coefficients are estimated
jointly with the regressions, in a one-step model rather than a regression on
assigned classes, so classification error does not attenuate them.

## Groups that share a class

When every row of a group belongs to the same class, pass `id` and
`class_level = "group"`. A group's evidence for a class is the product of its
rows' likelihoods, so classes of *students* are separated far more sharply
than classes of weeks could be. The binary `passed` outcome in these data
depends on the student's type, not on the week:

```{r group}
students <- mixture_regression(passed ~ hours, data = study_hours, n_classes = 2,
                               family = "binomial", id = "student",
                               class_level = "group", membership = ~ motivation,
                               n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
students
get_results(students, "membership")
```

Higher motivation lowers the odds of membership in the second class of
students (odds ratio 0.16 per standard deviation). With time as the
predictor, a mixture regression whose classes are shared by all measurements
of a person is latent class growth analysis, presented in the
[latent class growth analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/trajectory-classes.html)
article.

A mixture of Bernoulli distributions at a fixed covariate value is itself
Bernoulli, so identification needs additional structure. Covariate-dependent
logistic mixtures can be identifiable under suitable restrictions and covariate
support (Follmann and Lambert 1991). The implementation conservatively refuses
`family = "binomial"` with one trial per row unless the class is shared by a
group; this is its supported-model policy, not a universal nonidentification
theorem:

```{r not-identified, error = TRUE}
mixture_regression(passed ~ hours, data = study_hours, n_classes = 2,
                   family = "binomial")
```

## Two levels: groups that differ in their mix

The deep/surface strategy changes from week to week, but steady and erratic
students use the strategies in different proportions. That is a two-level
mixture (Vermunt 2003): rows keep their own regression class, and a latent
*group class* shifts the class probabilities of all rows in its groups.

```{r two-level}
two_level <- mixture_regression(score ~ hours, data = study_hours, n_classes = 2,
                                id = "student", n_group_classes = 2,
                                membership = ~ sleep, group_membership = ~ motivation,
                                n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
summary(two_level)
```

The `group_classes` table is the central result: within each group class,
the probability of each regression class. Students of group class 1 (51.3%)
follow the deep regression in 86.1% of their weeks, and students of group
class 2 (48.7%) the surface regression in 71.8%. The group-class membership
model shows motivation separating the two kinds of student (odds ratio 0.15
per standard deviation for group class 2), and the class model shows the week-level effect of
sleep.

```{r two-level-recovery}
get_results(two_level, "recovery", data = study_hours,
            truth = "student_type", by = "group_class")
```

Group class 1 contains 90.8% steady students and group class 2 89.2% erratic
students.

## Counts, shared effects and equal variances

The Poisson family takes counts, and `offset()` terms for exposure. `common`
names predictors whose coefficient is the same in every class; for the
Gaussian family `variance = "equal"` shares one residual standard deviation.

```{r counts}
asked <- mixture_regression(questions ~ hours + sleep, data = study_hours, n_classes = 2,
                            family = "poisson", common = ~ sleep, n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(asked, "coefficients")
```

The `Rate ratio` column (`exp_estimate` in the data frame) is the
exponentiated coefficient. Each hour of study multiplies the expected number
of questions by 1.11 in the first class and by 0.90 in the second, and the
shared effect of sleep (0.98) is not distinguishable from no effect.

## Uncertainty

Standard errors come from the observed information by default. Scores are
analytic (the posterior expectation of the complete-data score), and the
information is their numerical derivative. `vcov_type = "robust"` gives the
sandwich estimator with the CR1 small-sample factor `G / (G - 1)` for `G`
independent units, clustered on the independent unit: the row, or the group
when `id` defines one, including a single-level fit given `id`.

```{r robust}
get_results(fit, "coefficients", vcov_type = "robust")
plot(fit, what = "coefficients")
```

`p_adjusted` applies the Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the slopes.

## Prediction and simulation

`predict()` gives the class-averaged mean (`"response"`), every class's mean
(`"class_response"`), or, when the outcome is present, the posterior class
probabilities of new rows (`"posterior"`). `simulate()` draws new outcomes
from the fitted model, which is what the bootstrap test uses.

```{r predict}
new_weeks <- data.frame(hours = c(1, 6, 11))
predict(fit, new_weeks, type = "class_response")
```

## Checking a solution

Mixture likelihoods have local maxima. `mixture_regression()` starts EM from the
residuals of a pooled regression and from `n_starts` random partitions, and
the `starts` table shows how many starts reached the best likelihood. A
solution reached by one start only deserves more starts.

```{r starts}
get_results(fit, "starts")
plot(fit, what = "posteriors")
```

Every start reaches the log likelihood of -3144.01.

## How this compares with other software

The single-level and group-level models match `flexmix` (Leisch 2004): the
same likelihood at the same parameters, and the same binomial and Poisson
estimates. `flexmix` divides the Gaussian residual sum of squares by
`n - p`, so its Gaussian estimates are not quite the maximum-likelihood ones
and `mixture_regression()` can reach a slightly higher likelihood. The models
compared here use `flexmix` for single-level or shared-class grouped mixtures,
which differ from a two-level latent group-class model. `flexmix` provides
bootstrap likelihood-ratio tests through `LR_test()` and coefficient inference
through its refitting facilities.
